conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad we’re connecting today. My name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in caring for mothers in the weeks and months after birth (or adoption). Part of my role is to make sure every new parent feels seen, heard, and supported emotionally, because the transition to motherhood can be joyful and hard all at once.

To help me understand how you’ve been feeling lately, I’d like to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a well-studied tool that looks at mood, anxiety, and self-harm thoughts in the postpartum period. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your safety or the safety of someone else—then we’d talk together about the best next steps.

We’ll go through 10 gentle questions, and I’ll ask about the past seven days. There’s no right or wrong answer; just share what feels true for you. We can pause any time, and if something feels too hard to say out loud, just let me know and we’ll work around it.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has it been as much as always, a little less, almost never, or totally not at all?

Honestly? It’s been… a little less. I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would joke about the silliest things—but lately even the funny memes he shows me feel kind of flat. I’ll smile, but that easy laugh just doesn’t bubble up the way it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh, but it feels like I have to work for it. Most of the time I’m just too tired or preoccupied with the baby—worrying if he’s breathing okay, if I’m doing everything right. When something funny happens, I might chuckle for a second, but it fades fast and I’m right back to that heavy feeling in my chest.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park, even just binge-watching a show. Now I catch myself thinking “what’s the point?” or feeling like it’s too much effort to arrange. I still go, because I know I should, but that spark of “can’t wait” just isn’t there most days.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… way more than I should. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe my milk isn’t enough, or I missed his sleepy cues. The other night he wouldn’t settle and I kept replaying every little choice I’d made that day, convinced it was my fault. My head knows babies just cry, but I still hear this voice saying I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure something awful is about to happen—maybe the baby stopped breathing in the next room, or I’ll picture him slipping out of my arms. There’s no real trigger; the worry just barges in and I can’t shake it for a while. I check on him constantly, even when he’s sound asleep.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times this week. It hits suddenly—like yesterday when I was just warming a bottle and my chest got tight, heart pounding, felt like I couldn’t get a full breath. I knew rationally nothing was wrong, but my body kept screaming “something bad is about to happen.” It passes after a bit, but those minutes feel endless.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. Between the night feeds, the constant laundry, and trying to keep track of when he last ate or napped, I feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. Some mornings I just sit on the couch while he naps and stare at the mess, thinking, “Where do I even start?” I still get through the essentials, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying everything I might have done wrong, worrying about the next day, listening for every tiny noise from the bassinet. It takes me forever to drift off, and when I do, I’m up again at the slightest grunt. A few nights I’ve just stared at the ceiling until dawn, feeling this heavy knot of dread in my chest.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. It’s like a gray cloud parked over me—nothing feels bright. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start sliding down without warning. I look at him and feel guilty because I *know* I’m supposed to be grateful, but the sadness is still there, tucked right under my ribs.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened maybe three or four times this week. Sometimes it’s because I’m overwhelmed—like when he wouldn’t latch and I felt useless—but other times it’s nothing specific. I’ll just be rocking him and the tears start. I try to stay quiet so he won’t see, but it’s hard to stop once it starts.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. My baby needs me, and I want to be here for him, even on the hardest days.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: POSTPARTUM MOOD/ANXIETY SCREENING NOTE

Symptoms endorsed (≥ 7 days/week unless noted)
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Anxious preoccupations (infant safety, catastrophizing)  
- Panic-type episodes (tight chest, racing heart)  
- Sleep disturbance secondary to intrusive worry/sadness  
- Feeling overwhelmed and “drowning” in daily tasks  
- Crying spells 3–4×/week, sometimes spontaneous  

Patterns
- Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, for ≥ 2 weeks  
- Functional impact: difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep, avoidance of previously enjoyed activities, perceived low coping capacity  

Screening significance  
High likelihood of Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset; comorbid anxiety symptoms (possible Panic Disorder, GAD)  

Risk factors  
- Postpartum period (≤ 12 mos)  
- Mood-congruent insomnia  
- Recurrent inappropriate guilt  
- No self-harm ideation reported; therefore, acute suicidal risk absent at screening  

Overall impression  
Responses place patient above standard EPDS cut-off for probable postpartum depression; recommend formal diagnostic interview and stepped-care planning.
